This tutorial walks through a complete meta-analysis in R, from pooling the studies to
checking whether the evidence is actually conclusive. It covers the two data formats you
will meet most often when extracting data from trials:

| Outcome type | What you extract per group | Effect measure | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Binary** (dichotomous) | number of **events** and **total** participants | Risk ratio (RR) | BCG vaccine and tuberculosis |
| **Continuous** | **mean**, **SD** and **n** | Standardized mean difference (SMD) or mean difference (MD) | Asthma education and days off work |

**Every code box is live**: press **Run Code** to execute it in your browser, then edit the
code and run it again. Nothing needs to be installed.

::: {.callout-note}
## First run takes a few seconds
The page downloads R and the packages (`metafor`, `RTSA`) the first time. Wait until the
status at the top of the page says it's ready, then run the boxes **in order**: each box
uses objects created by the ones above it.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(metafor)
library(RTSA)
```

# Part A: Binary outcomes (events and total)

## A1. Enter the data

For each trial, extract the number of **events** and the **total** number of participants
in the experimental group (`event.e`, `n.e`) and the control group (`event.c`, `n.c`).
This example uses 13 trials of the **BCG vaccine** for preventing tuberculosis. We also
record two study characteristics to use later: how participants were allocated (`alloc`)
and the absolute latitude of the study site (`ablat`).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use your own data
Replace the numbers below with your own studies, keeping the same column names. In
RStudio you can also read them from a spreadsheet: `bin <- read.csv("my_data.csv")`.
:::

```{webr-r}
bin <- data.frame(
  study   = c("Aronson 1948", "Ferguson & Simes 1949", "Rosenthal et al 1960",
              "Hart & Sutherland 1977", "Frimodt-Moller et al 1973",
              "Stein & Aronson 1953", "Vandiviere et al 1973", "TPT Madras 1980",
              "Coetzee & Berjak 1968", "Rosenthal et al 1961", "Comstock et al 1974",
              "Comstock & Webster 1969", "Comstock et al 1976"),
  year    = c(1948, 1949, 1960, 1977, 1973, 1953, 1973, 1980, 1968, 1961, 1974, 1969, 1976),
  event.e = c(4, 6, 3, 62, 33, 180, 8, 505, 29, 17, 186, 5, 27),
  n.e     = c(123, 306, 231, 13598, 5069, 1541, 2545, 88391, 7499, 1716, 50634, 2498, 16913),
  event.c = c(11, 29, 11, 248, 47, 372, 10, 499, 45, 65, 141, 3, 29),
  n.c     = c(139, 303, 220, 12867, 5808, 1451, 629, 88391, 7277, 1665, 27338, 2341, 17854),
  alloc   = c("random", "random", "random", "random", "alternate", "alternate", "random",
              "random", "random", "systematic", "systematic", "systematic", "systematic"),
  ablat   = c(44, 55, 42, 52, 13, 44, 19, 13, 27, 42, 18, 33, 33)
)
bin
```

## A2. Calculate effect sizes

`escalc()` computes an effect size and its sampling variance for each study. With events
and totals, give it `ai`/`n1i` (experimental) and `ci`/`n2i` (control). We use the
**log risk ratio** (`measure = "RR"`). Ratios are pooled on the log scale and converted back
at the end. Use `measure = "OR"` for odds ratios or `"RD"` for risk differences.

```{webr-r}
dat <- escalc(measure = "RR",
              ai = event.e, n1i = n.e,   # experimental: events, total
              ci = event.c, n2i = n.c,   # control:      events, total
              data = bin, slab = study)
dat[, c("study", "yi", "vi")]
```

`yi` is the log risk ratio and `vi` its variance. A negative `yi` means fewer TB cases
in the vaccinated group.

## A3. Random-effects meta-analysis

Trials differ in populations and settings, so we assume the true effect varies between
studies and fit a **random-effects model** (REML estimator, the `metafor` default).

```{webr-r}
res <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML")
res
```

Convert the pooled estimate back to a risk ratio, with its 95% CI and prediction interval:

```{webr-r}
predict(res, transf = exp, digits = 2)
```

**How to read it:**

- **Pooled RR ≈ 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.70):** on average, vaccination roughly halves the risk of TB.
- **I² ≈ 92% and Q-test p < 0.0001:** heterogeneity is very high. The trials disagree a lot
  more than chance would explain.
- **95% prediction interval ≈ 0.15 to 1.55:** a *new* trial could find anything from a large
  benefit to no benefit. With this much heterogeneity, the prediction interval matters as much
  as the pooled estimate.

### Forest plot

```{webr-r}
forest(res, atransf = exp,
       header = c("Study", "RR [95% CI]"),
       xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
```

## A4. Subgroup analysis

Does the effect differ by **allocation method** (random, alternate, systematic)? First,
pool the studies within each subgroup separately:

```{webr-r}
for (g in c("random", "alternate", "systematic")) {
  r <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, subset = alloc == g)
  cat(sprintf("%-11s k = %2d   RR = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]   I2 = %.0f%%\n",
              g, r$k, exp(r$b), exp(r$ci.lb), exp(r$ci.ub), r$I2))
}
```

Then test whether the subgroups **differ from each other**. Adding `alloc` as a moderator
gives the test for subgroup differences (the `QM` statistic):

```{webr-r}
sub <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ alloc, data = dat)
sub
```

The test of moderators gives **QM ≈ 1.77, df = 2, p ≈ 0.41**: no evidence that the effect
differs by allocation method. The subgroup estimates look different, but the differences
are compatible with chance.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Good practice for subgroups
Pre-specify subgroups in your protocol, keep them few, and judge them by the **test for
subgroup differences**, not by whether one subgroup is "significant" and another isn't.
:::

### Meta-regression: a continuous moderator

Subgroups split studies into categories. For a continuous characteristic such as
**latitude**, use meta-regression:

```{webr-r}
mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = dat)
mr
regplot(mr, transf = exp, xlab = "Absolute latitude (degrees)", ylab = "Risk ratio")
```

Latitude is strongly associated with the effect (**p < 0.0001**) and explains about
**76% of the heterogeneity** (R²). The vaccine works better further from the equator.

## A5. Publication bias

Small studies with "negative" results are less likely to be published, which can make the
pooled effect look too good. Start with a **funnel plot**: without bias, the studies
should scatter symmetrically around the pooled estimate.

```{webr-r}
funnel(res, xlab = "Log risk ratio")
```

Then use formal tests:

```{webr-r}
regtest(res)    # Egger's regression test
ranktest(res)   # Begg's rank correlation test
```

Neither test suggests asymmetry (Egger p ≈ 0.42, Begg p ≈ 0.95).

**Trim-and-fill** estimates how many studies might be "missing" and adds them to see
how the result would change:

```{webr-r}
tf <- trimfill(res)
tf
funnel(tf, xlab = "Log risk ratio")   # filled studies are shown as open circles
predict(tf, transf = exp, digits = 2)
```

One study is imputed, and the adjusted RR (≈ 0.52) barely moves, so the conclusion holds.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Interpret with care
These tests have low power with fewer than about 10 studies, and funnel asymmetry can
come from heterogeneity, not just publication bias. Here, heterogeneity is very high, so
treat all of these results as rough checks.
:::

## A6. Trial sequential analysis (TSA)

A conventional meta-analysis can look "significant" just because it was tested repeatedly
as trials accumulated, or because there isn't yet enough information. **TSA** treats the
meta-analysis like a sequential trial. It calculates the **required information size**
(the number of participants needed for a reliable answer) and draws **monitoring
boundaries** that the cumulative Z-curve must cross before you can call the result firm.

We use the [`RTSA`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RTSA) package. For binary outcomes
it needs the columns `eI`, `nI` (intervention events, total) and `eC`, `nC` (control
events, total), with trials in **chronological order**:

```{webr-r}
tsa_bin <- with(bin[order(bin$year), ],
                data.frame(study, eI = event.e, nI = n.e, eC = event.c, nC = n.c))
tsa_bin
```

Now run the TSA. We assume a minimal clinically relevant effect of **RR = 0.8**
(a 20% relative risk reduction), α = 5% (two-sided) and 80% power, with O'Brien-Fleming
alpha-spending boundaries:

```{webr-r}
tsa <- RTSA(type = "analysis", data = tsa_bin, outcome = "RR",
            mc = 0.8,              # minimal clinically relevant RR
            side = 2, alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.2,
            es_alpha = "esOF",     # O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending
            fixed = FALSE)         # random-effects
tsa
```

```{webr-r}
suppressWarnings(print(plot(tsa)))   # hides harmless ggplot2 warnings
```

**How to read it:**

- The conventional random-effects result is "significant" (naive **p ≈ 0.002**).
- But with this much heterogeneity and a low event rate, the **required information size
  is huge**: about 3.5 million participants. The trials provide only about **10%** of it.
- The **TSA-adjusted 95% CI (≈ 0.01 to 18)** is extremely wide, and the Z-curve hasn't crossed
  the monitoring boundary.

So, by TSA standards, this body of evidence is **not yet conclusive**, even though the
ordinary meta-analysis looks clear. This is exactly the situation TSA is designed to
flag: an apparently significant result that rests on too little information once
heterogeneity is accounted for.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
Change `mc = 0.8` to `mc = 0.5` (you're now only interested in halving the risk) and run
the box again. How does the required information size change?
:::

# Part B: Continuous outcomes (mean, SD and n)

## B1. Enter the data

For continuous outcomes, extract the **mean**, **standard deviation** and **number of
participants** in each group: `mean.e`, `sd.e`, `n.e` (experimental) and `mean.c`,
`sd.c`, `n.c` (control).

This example uses 13 trials of **self-management education for adults with asthma**
(Gibson et al. 2002, from the `metadat` package). The outcome is the number of **days off
work or school**, so lower is better. The `program` column records whether the
intervention was **optimal** self-management (written action plan, self-monitoring and
regular medical review) or only **partial**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Check your SDs
Papers often report the **standard error (SE)** or a **95% CI** instead of the SD.
Convert them first: SD = SE × √n, or, for a 95% CI of a mean, SD = √n × (upper − lower) / 3.92.
Entering an SE as an SD is one of the most common errors in meta-analysis.
:::

```{webr-r}
cont <- data.frame(
  study   = c("Cote 1997", "Ghosh 1998", "Hayward 1996", "Heard 1999",
              "Ignacio-Garcia 1995", "Knoell 1998", "Lahdensuo 1996", "Sommaruga 1995",
              "Zeiger 1991", "Garret 1994", "Neri 1996", "Hilton 1986", "Gallefoss 1999"),
  year    = c(1997, 1998, 1996, 1999, 1995, 1998, 1996, 1995, 1991, 1994, 1996, 1986, 1999),
  mean.e  = c(2.2, 17.6, 0.38, 2.09, 4.92, 0.85, 2.8, 24.1, 1.4, 6.23, 2.1, 0.73, 8),
  sd.e    = c(12.73, 24.2, 0.56, 5.93, 6.05, 4.75, 9, 11.8, 3.3, 12.2, 8, 1.48, 32),
  n.e     = c(50, 140, 23, 97, 35, 45, 56, 20, 128, 119, 32, 86, 25),
  mean.c  = c(5.2, 34.1, 0.23, 2.66, 20, 2.31, 4.8, 31.8, 2.3, 5.71, 5.1, 0.47, 26),
  sd.c    = c(12.5, 38.8, 0.29, 4.95, 26.34, 9.16, 7.2, 17.9, 7.6, 8.57, 14, 1.2, 70),
  n.c     = c(54, 136, 19, 94, 35, 55, 59, 20, 143, 100, 33, 100, 24),
  program = c(rep("optimal", 9), rep("partial", 4))
)
cont
```

## B2. Calculate effect sizes: SMD or MD?

- Use the **mean difference (MD)** when all studies measure the outcome **on the same
  scale** in the same way. It keeps the original units (here, days).
- Use the **standardized mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g)** when studies use different
  scales or instruments, or when the spread differs a lot between studies.

Here, the trials measured days off over very different follow-up periods (look at the means:
from under 1 day to over 30), so, like the original review, we use the **SMD**:

```{webr-r}
dat_c <- escalc(measure = "SMD",            # use "MD" for mean difference
                m1i = mean.e, sd1i
= sd.e, n1i = n.e,   # experimental
                m2i = mean.c, sd2i = sd.c, n2i = n.c,   # control
                data = cont, slab = study)
dat_c[, c("study", "yi", "vi")]
```

A negative SMD means **fewer days off** in the education group. As a rough guide, an SMD of
0.2 is a small effect, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.

## B3. Random-effects meta-analysis

```{webr-r}
res_c <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat_c)
res_c
predict(res_c, digits = 2)
```

```{webr-r}
forest(res_c, header = c("Study", "SMD [95% CI]"),
       xlab = "Standardized mean difference (Hedges' g)")
```

**How to read it:**

- **Pooled SMD ≈ −0.19 (95% CI −0.34 to −0.05), p ≈ 0.01:** self-management education
  slightly reduces days off work or school. This is a small effect.
- **I² ≈ 54%, Q-test p ≈ 0.008:** moderate heterogeneity.
- **95% prediction interval ≈ −0.60 to 0.21:** in a new setting, the effect could range from a
  moderate benefit to none.

## B4. Subgroup analysis

Is **optimal** self-management more effective than **partial** programs?

```{webr-r}
for (g in c("optimal", "partial")) {
  r <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat_c, subset = program == g)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s k = %d   SMD = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]   I2 = %.0f%%\n",
              g, r$k, r$b, r$ci.lb, r$ci.ub, r$I2))
}
sub_c <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ program, data = dat_c)
sub_c
```

The optimal programs show a small benefit (**SMD ≈ −0.27, 95% CI −0.43 to −0.11**), while
the partial programs show none (**SMD ≈ 0.01**). The test for subgroup differences is
borderline (**QM ≈ 3.57, p ≈ 0.06**), and the partial subgroup has only 4 trials, so this
is a hypothesis to test in future trials, not a firm conclusion.

## B5. Publication bias

```{webr-r}
funnel(res_c, xlab = "Hedges' g")
regtest(res_c)
ranktest(res_c)
```

Neither Egger's test (p ≈ 0.52) nor Begg's test (p ≈ 0.37) is significant. But look at
trim-and-fill:

```{webr-r}
tf_c <- trimfill(res_c)
tf_c
funnel(tf_c, xlab = "Hedges' g")
```

Trim-and-fill imputes **4 missing studies** on the right (no benefit) side, and the
adjusted SMD shrinks to **≈ −0.07 (95% CI −0.24 to 0.10)**, which is no longer significant.
So the small benefit is **sensitive to possible small-study effects**, even though the
formal tests were negative. This is worth reporting as a limitation.

## B6. Trial sequential analysis (TSA)

For continuous outcomes, `RTSA` works on the **mean difference in the original units**
(days). It needs `mI`, `sdI`, `nI` (intervention) and `mC`, `sdC`, `nC` (control), in
chronological order:

```{webr-r}
tsa_cont <- with(cont[order(cont$year), ],
                 data.frame(study, mI = mean.e, sdI = sd.e, nI = n.e,
                                   mC = mean.c, sdC = sd.c, nC = n.c))
```

For a continuous TSA you need two assumptions: the **minimal relevant difference** (`mc`)
and the expected **SD** of the outcome (`sd_mc`). Here we look for a reduction of
**1 day** off work, with an SD of 8 days:

```{webr-r}
tsa_c <- RTSA(type = "analysis", data = tsa_cont, outcome = "MD",
              mc = -1,           # minimal relevant difference: 1 day fewer
              sd_mc = 8,         # expected SD of days off
              side = 2, alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.2,
              es_alpha = "esOF", fixed = FALSE)
tsa_c
suppressWarnings(print(plot(tsa_c)))
```

**How to read it:**

- The pooled mean difference is **≈ −0.8 days (TSA-adjusted 95% CI −2.08 to 0.48)**.
- The trials provide about **51% of the required information size** (≈ 1,728 of 3,361
  participants).
- The Z-curve crosses neither the conventional (green) nor the TSA (red) boundary.

So there isn't yet enough information to confirm or rule out a 1-day reduction: more
trials are needed.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why is the MD here different from a REML model?
`RTSA` uses the DerSimonian-Laird (DL) estimator for random effects. Run
`rma(yi, vi, data = escalc("MD", m1i = mean.e, sd1i = sd.e, n1i = n.e, m2i = mean.c, sd2i = sd.c, n2i = n.c, data = cont), method = "DL")`
and you get the same −0.79 days. With `method = "REML"` you get about −2.5 days, because
these trials differ so much in scale. When results depend this much on the estimator,
report it as a sensitivity analysis, and it's another reason the SMD was the better
primary measure here.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Limitation of these examples
TSA is meant to be planned prospectively. Running it after the fact, as here, is a
sensitivity analysis, and `RTSA` warns about this in its output.
:::

# Summary

| Step | Function | Binary: BCG trials (RR) | Continuous: asthma education (SMD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data | `data.frame()` | events and total per group | mean, SD and n per group |
| Effect sizes | `escalc()` | `measure = "RR"` | `measure = "SMD"` |
| Pooled effect | `rma()` | RR 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70), I² ≈ 92% | SMD −0.19 (−0.34 to −0.05), I² ≈ 54% |
| Subgroups | `rma(mods = ~ group)` | No difference by allocation (p ≈ 0.41) | Optimal vs partial, borderline (p ≈ 0.06) |
| Publication bias | `funnel()`, `regtest()`, `ranktest()`, `trimfill()` | No clear asymmetry; adjusted RR ≈ 0.52 | Tests negative, but trim-and-fill removes the effect |
| TSA | `RTSA()` | ≈ 10% of required information; not conclusive | ≈ 51% of required information; not conclusive |

# Run it on your own computer

Everything above also works in regular R or RStudio. Install the packages once:

```r
install.packages(c("metafor", "RTSA"))
```

Then copy the code from each box, in order. To use your own studies, replace the numbers in
the `bin` or `cont` data frame (or read them from a spreadsheet with `read.csv()`) and keep
the column names.
